extracted.intended_audience: graduate students, researchers, and scholars in paleontology, evolutionary biology, and history/philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative criteria for constructing, selecting, and evaluating models and research agendas in paleontology (the 'science of form'), including methodological precepts, standards for model choice, and disciplinary aims. Useful for reviewers, historians/philosophers of science, and researchers designing paleontological studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin inquiry at the appropriate level / favor idealized models
rubrics_metrics.description: "Idealized models are favored over actual specimens" (Gould 1970b, 77). The methodological precept is to construct models of evolutionary processes—specifically the optimizing process of adaptation—so inquiry can focus on properties of adaptation in general rather than morphological change of a particular taxon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use idealized, process-focused models to study immanent processes that produce events rather than on the events themselves; this nomothetic orientation lets paleontologists target general laws rather than descriptive, taxon-specific generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simplicity and interpretability over maximizing fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate statistical fit is important but not the only attribute of a "good" formula: prefer "a reasonably simple functional expression involving the minimum of non-interpretable parameters" (Sholl 1954, 225, quoted; Gould 1966 discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adding terms to improve fit if they sacrifice parameter interpretability and range of applicability. Prioritize functional forms that yield interpretable parameters and broad applicability across multiple cases rather than case-specific curve-fitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate statistical fit is necessary but secondary to generality and interpretability
rubrics_metrics.description: "Adequate statistical fit, while certainly the most important consideration... is not the only attribute" of a good model (discussion of Gould 1966). A model's quantitative accuracy can be less important than its ability to be interpreted and generalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating models, weigh simplicity, interpretability, and generalizability alongside measures of fit; beware models that fit a particular fossil series well but provide uninterpretable parameters and limited explanatory reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models should aim to reveal laws and mechanistic underpinnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Model-based approaches have superior talent for uncovering laws and allow us to understand the mechanical or biological underpinnings of those laws, fostering extension of models to other systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess models for their capacity to generate nomothetic generalizations and mechanistic insight; successful models should permit plausible extension to other domains where similar influences operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test functional hypotheses with optimality models to support causal claims about adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Testing the functional hypothesis is the best approach because its rival cannot be proven" (Gould 1970b, quoting Raup). Positive fit to an optimality model suggests adaptation to a specific function; lack of fit suggests lack of adaptation to that function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct explicit optimality/functional models specifying function a priori; test multiple plausible functions; interpret fits and mismatches as evidence for or against adaptive explanations rather than relying on narrative inference alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimality modeling is required to demonstrate adaptive function (and non-optimality) rigorously
rubrics_metrics.description: Optimality models clarify what it takes to demonstrate adaptive function and are uniquely capable of demonstrating deviation from design, provided the function can be specified a priori (discussion of Rudwick and Gould).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that without a specified optimality model, claims of adaptation are weak. Use properly formulated optimality models to distinguish adaptation from phylogenetic accident or other explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'just-so' storytelling; require quantitative models and explicit assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of narratives that lack quantitative optimality models (Gould's antler-size discussion): without quantitative models and their predictions, explanations can devolve into speculative "just-so" stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand explicit models, quantitative predictions, and clear assumptions when inferring adaptive explanations; treat speculative narrative explanations skeptically unless grounded in testable modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select research problems that have broad demand to achieve disciplinary significance
rubrics_metrics.description: A discipline must identify problems "whose solution was in sufficiently high demand"; the science of form failed partly because it focused on demonstrating a mechanism (natural selection) whose central importance was already accepted and so did not address problems in high demand (Gould quote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For research programs seeking disciplinary autonomy or broad impact, prioritize questions whose answers are widely sought across the community and that can generate new, expansive generalizations rather than only refining accepted mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to generate new theory and expansive generalizations, not just valuable case studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Much functional morphology produced elegant, useful studies of particular taxa but "will furnish no new or expansive generalizations" (Gould). Excess case-focused work, even if valuable, may not advance general theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating research, prefer projects that articulate and test hypotheses with potential to produce general principles; treat single-taxon descriptive studies as valuable but limited in their capacity to found a new theoretical program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate non-optimality and constraints as central, general problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Gould suggests the science of form will fulfill its promise by probing situations "in which animals are not well designed"—developmental, phyletic, and architectural constraints as marks of history are key issues (Gould 1980, quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage studies that explain clumping and sparse occupation of morphospace, exploring historical constraints and non-adaptive explanations; such problems can yield general laws and broader theoretical import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of conceptual lenses and biases (e.g., phyletic gradualism) that filter data interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Eldredge criticized the unconscious guidance of phyletic gradualism, which causes paleontologists to interpret fossil data through a gradualist lens rather than treating alternative models (e.g., allopatric speciation) as viable explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine default assumptions or paradigms that shape data interpretation; explicitly consider alternative models (e.g., saltation, allopatric speciation) when interpreting patterns like stasis or rapid change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure figures and illustrations faithfully represent a model's theoretical commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique that Eldredge's depiction of the allopatric model made it seem to imply stasis as necessary, although allopatric speciation itself does not specify long-term stasis; illustrations can mislead about a model's commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using diagrams/figures to communicate models, carefully represent what the model does and does not claim; avoid schematic choices that conflate distinct mechanisms or imply causal necessity not entailed by the theory.
